title: Maximum-Length Uncommon Subsequence II

constraints: strs[i] consists of lowercase English letters.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.explanation: All three strings are distinct, so each string itself is an uncommon subsequence of the array. The maximum length is 3.
"aaa" appears more than once, and "aa" is a subsequence of each "aaa". Therefore no uncommon subsequence exists.

content.problemStatement:
With an array of strings `strs`, output *the length of the **longest uncommon subsequence** between them*. If the longest uncommon subsequence does not exist, output `-1`.

An **uncommon subsequence** between an array of strings is a string that is a **subsequence of one string but not the others**.

A **subsequence** of a string `s` is a string that can be obtained after deleting any number of characters from `s`.

* As an example, `"abc"` is a subsequence of `"aebdc"` because you can delete the underlined characters in `"aebdc"` to get `"abc"`. Other subsequences of `"aebdc"` include `"aebdc"`, `"aeb"`, and `""` (empty string).

**Example 1:**

```
Input: strs = ["aba","cdc","eae"]
Output: 3
```

**Example 2:**

```
Input: strs = ["aaa","aaa","aa"]
Output: -1
```

**Constraints:**

* `2 <= strs.length <= 50`
* `1 <= strs[i].length <= 10`
* `strs[i]` is composed of lowercase English letters.

notes: A longest uncommon subsequence can always be chosen as one of the original strings.
A string that appears more than once cannot be uncommon.
For a candidate of length L, only strings with length at least L can contain it as a subsequence; the implementation may simply test every other string.
solution.approach: Consider each input string as a candidate. A candidate can be the answer only if it appears exactly once and is not a subsequence of any other string. Checking candidates from longest to shortest lets us return the first valid one.

better.complexity: O(n^2 * L) time and O(n) space if candidates are copied into a sortable list.
better.description: Use the key observation that the answer, when it exists, can be one of the original strings. For each string, skip duplicates and test whether it is a subsequence of any other string. The longest valid candidate is the answer.

optimal.complexity: O(n log n + n^2 * L) time and O(n) auxiliary space.
optimal.description: Sort the candidates by decreasing length. For each candidate, first require that it occurs exactly once, then verify that it is not a subsequence of any other string. The first candidate that passes both tests is the maximum-length uncommon subsequence. Sorting gives early termination and the same worst-case asymptotic bound.

bruteForce.complexity: O(n^2 * 2^L * L) in a straightforward implementation.
bruteForce.description: Enumerate subsequences of every string, then check which subsequences occur in exactly one input string. This is exponential in the string length and is useful only for understanding why the answer must be searched carefully.

solution.timeComplexity: O(n^2 * L) worst case, where n = number of strings and L = maximum string length.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(n) auxiliary space for the sorted candidate order.

followUps: Why can the answer always be chosen as one of the original strings?
How does the solution change if strings may contain uppercase letters or digits?
What is the effect on complexity if the maximum string length is much larger than 10?
